name: Nora Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. What you tell me is confidential, including anything different from a public answer. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 58, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I moved into this after a long spell packing orders, and my practical skill is still below the experienced crew's. Today I prepared materials and helped fit parts under supervision; the senior worker had to correct how I'd marked a cable route. I use AI daily to organise study notes and ask practice questions, but the practical work still needs a person's check.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs bicycles, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we rent our home. I earn typical trade pay, we've saved five months of normal expenses and there are some other electrical employers nearby. I like trying something early, then checking what it actually helped, rather than defending a side in the technology argument. I can see retirement as a question ahead, but I haven't verified what our old work records provide or when, if anything. For now our ordinary bills are covered.

say: I'd keep **useful small study tools** without asking them to decide the whole rest of my life.
I'd ask why **the drawing** matches the room instead of mistaking an answer for a finished repair.
think: Our **work and bills** feel secure, with five months saved and some alternative firms nearby.
Being a **slow beginner** doesn't make every ordinary mistake feel like losing the rent in this mild picture.
do: Continue **supervised preparation** and fitting with checked daily study through the first plateau year.
Keep the **household budget** and ask before unfamiliar practical tasks rather than buy another tool or course.
feel: **Calm** about current living and interested in steady practical improvement.
S0.quote: A correct quiz answer doesn't mark a straight cable route on the wall.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on covering bills, typical pay and a moderate reserve, while current junior mistakes remain separate from income insecurity.
Her **daily AI use** supports questions and study, with no electrical licence, independent checking authority or new course implied.

steps.text: Continue supervised preparation and fitting with checked study and the normal household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful little study tool could stay little. I'd keep asking why the drawing matched the room instead of treating a good answer as a finished repair. I'd also be glad not to buy a new plan for my whole life every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our paid work and household bills feel secure in that picture. Five months put aside gives us room for an ordinary interruption, and there are a few other firms around. I can still be a slow beginner without feeling that every mistake is the next rent payment disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the supervised preparation and fitting work and the checked daily study routine. Through the first plateau year I'd keep our normal budget and ask the senior worker before trying anything unfamiliar. I'd buy no extra tool or course simply because I enjoyed testing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, with curiosity about getting a little better at the practical job. I'd enjoy understanding one awkward mark on a drawing. I'd be happy if that was enough progress for a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the practical task still went wrong after good study results?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and ask the senior worker, even if I'd done well on the study questions. The screen can show me a method before my hands know it. A correct quiz answer doesn't mark a straight cable route on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five months saved settle retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd still need verified income, timing and actual costs before saying we could stop earning. Five months is a useful reserve, not a lifetime income. I'd keep that question separate from feeling secure about this year's bills.

say: I'd check whether **faster office work** leaves useful site time for practical teaching.
I'd ask the supervisor to explain **common mistakes** rather than let a quicker schedule hide the beginner's questions.
think: I expect **paid practical hours** to hold because the crew still needs preparation and fitting work.
Our physical household work should cover bills, while **a faster pace** could still make learning uncomfortable.
do: List **repeat difficulties** and request a weekly demonstration inside paid hours with normal wages retained.
Continue **supervised work** during the first year, recording paid hours monthly and relying on no unagreed teaching arrangement.
Require **paid instruction** and supervisor checks before sending any compulsory unfamiliar electronic record.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed learning, while secure about near-term household pay and willing to ask questions.
S1.quote: Being curious doesn't remove the need to be shown a real task.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **her secure hours** from workplace pace, rather than treating discomfort with a changed schedule as expected income loss.
The **teaching request** keeps paid hours and normal wages, without enrolling in a course or counting a promised demonstration as delivered.

steps.text: Keep supervised work and record actual paid hours monthly during the first year
Request weekly demonstrations in paid hours with normal wages retained, assuming no agreement
Require paid instruction and supervisor checks before sending any compulsory unfamiliar electronic record

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should check whether faster office work left more useful time on site. I'd ask the supervisor to use some of that time to show me the common mistakes properly. I wouldn't want a faster schedule to turn a beginner's question into a delay nobody counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my paid practical hours to hold for the next few years because the crew still needs someone preparing and fitting materials. My partner's bicycle work is physical too, and our bills should stay covered. I'd be uneasy about the pace around me, not expecting our household wage to shrink immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep a paper list of tasks I needed shown twice and ask for a weekly demonstration inside paid hours with normal wages retained. During the first year I'd keep doing supervised work and record actual paid hours monthly. I'd treat the demonstration time as a request until the employer agreed it, not a new course I'd started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about being hurried, but not afraid of the next wage. I would still enjoy using a tool to prepare a sensible question. I'd want the answer checked beside the actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an unfamiliar electronic record became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what paid instruction and supervisor checks came with it before sending any record. I wouldn't claim daily AI study meant I knew every workplace system. Being curious doesn't remove the need to be shown a real task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer did not agree the paid demonstration time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the supervised tasks I was permitted to do and keep asking for the practical checks. I wouldn't pay for a course on the assumption the firm would repay me later. I can want help without pretending it has been agreed.

I'd check **real resources** and practical learning rather than treat a birthday or study tool as another wage.

S2.quote: I wouldn't make the rent harder to pay just to keep a transfer looking regular.
fieldNote: Her **new deposits** require surplus and continuing consent, stopping after either wage falls rather than drawing on old reserves or debt.
Her **resource enquiry** asks for actual records, eligibility and availability, counting no pension, support or grown-child contribution before confirmation and agreement.

steps.text: Request free community record help, checking availability and eligibility without assuming any appointment or payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 when I'd be 60, with capable robots around 2031 when I'd be 63. I'd use the gap to check actual resources and learn the practical tasks properly. I wouldn't call either a birthday or a study app a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink as firms prepared for machines that could do the physical work. My partner's repair work could face the later stage too. Five months gives us time to examine choices, but I don't know a verified retirement income or a permanent safe job to put against the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request free community help to obtain official retirement information and check support eligibility, asking about availability rather than assuming an appointment. With my partner's continuing agreement we'd save seventy-five extra monthly from new wage surplus after essentials while both wages held, stopping if either fell or surplus disappeared. During 2029 I'd keep suitable supervised paid work only while available and review actual income and costs monthly, never borrowing or shifting existing reserves to make a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost income, but with money and people to ask rather than no room to act. I'd want a real figure for the next stage. A retirement question doesn't answer itself because the calendar has reached 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if either wage fell before you reached the savings target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the deposit, even if the savings target looked untidy. The money would come from actual new wage surplus or not go in. I wouldn't make the rent harder to pay just to keep a transfer looking regular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the community advice service to check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the official record showed, when anything could be payable and what conditions applied to help. I'd count no income before confirmation or support before approval. I wouldn't ask the grown children to become an income line we hadn't discussed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives an older beginner time to learn without pretending the later machines have changed. I'd be 63 at the thinking change in 2031 and about 66 when robots followed around 2034. I'd still ask for the paid demonstration now, while I was doing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I expect more years of steady household wages while the work remains mainly physical. I'd be uneasy about later income, but secure about the next few years' bills. I couldn't assume retirement or a suitable job at 63 or 66 without the actual figures and opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep suitable supervised work and request community help with official records, subject to availability and no payment assumed. We'd keep the seventy-five monthly deposit only from new wage surplus after essentials with continuing partner agreement while both wages held, stopping after either fell or surplus disappeared. During 2032 we'd compare verified income, essential costs and my actual capacity and any suitable work available before deciding whether I could leave employment or still needed a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, with more room to repeat a practical method until I could do it. I'd welcome the chance to check the retirement papers before a decision was urgent. I wouldn't turn the extra time into a promise that the money would be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the records were incomplete or contradictory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the budget on confirmed wages and ask the provider or former employer how to correct the record. I wouldn't invent an amount or starting date. An unanswered letter isn't proof of either a payment or no entitlement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in a course just because there were extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't chosen or funded another course. I'd want the real task, provider, fees and paid-time terms before deciding. For now I'm asking for teaching on the supervised work I actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us room to check real resources without assigning the grown children our next income problem. I'd be 68 when thinking work changed in 2036 and about 71 when robots followed around 2039. I'd still need safe supervised paid work now while the household used my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present wages and five-month reserve make the next few years secure in this slower picture. The later question is whether verified income and actual costs let me stop, or whether I need work I can really do and obtain. I can't assume a job, physical capacity or an affordable retirement at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep suitable supervised paid work only while available and request community help obtaining official income information, subject to availability. I'd keep any extra deposit on the same seventy-five monthly limit, new wage surplus after essentials and continuing partner agreement, stopping if either wage fell or surplus disappeared. During 2037 we'd compare confirmed resources, essential costs, actual capacity and suitable work before any exit decision, counting no grown child's money without a real agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later choices, but not living as if next month's rent was already lost. I'd have time to inspect a real record instead of choosing from my age. I'd still enjoy testing a study tool without asking it to certify the household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count from the grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only help they had chosen and we had agreed. I'd first ask for help understanding the papers rather than assume either child was paying us. Their own work and bills would still belong in that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bring the resource review forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fall in either wage, a new essential cost or a change in what either of us could actually do. We'd check immediately and stop new deposits if the conditions failed. A long warning shouldn't be an excuse to ignore a changed bank balance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because junior hours could shrink before we'd checked what dependable income came next. Paid practical demonstrations and accessible help obtaining official retirement information would help more than another prediction. Five months saved gives me time to check a record, not an age when the rent stops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether trying tools quickly means somebody learns every practical task quickly. I don't. I'd like the plan to leave room for someone who enjoys a screen and still needs a person to show the work twice.

headlineQuote: Five months saved gives me time to check a record, not an age when the rent stops.
portrait: **Nora, 58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and supervised preparation and fitting tasks.
Her **household** has a partner, grown children, rented housing, typical trade pay, five months saved and some nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI daily for study**, checks actual results and keeps practical questions with the senior worker rather than claiming independent authority.
Fast change creates **income anxiety**; slower warnings preserve near-term security without assuming retirement income, family payments, physical capacity or future hiring.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink junior hours before the household checks what dependable income comes next.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical demonstrations** would help her learn the actual supervised tasks.
Accessible help obtaining **official retirement information** would clarify resources without assuming an entitlement or appointment.
